texts: A calcified aortic valve with a mean gradient of 24 mmHg, a velocity of 2.6 m/s and an ejection fraction of 25% is low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis, and the next test is a dobutamine stress echo.
A weak ventricle may fail to open a moderately diseased valve, so it looks severe (pseudo-severe stenosis), or it may be too weak to push a high gradient through a truly severe valve.
Low-dose dobutamine raises the flow: if the gradient rises and the valve area stays small, the stenosis is truly severe; if the area opens up, it is pseudo-severe.
It also shows whether the ventricle has contractile reserve, which predicts the result of valve replacement.
Thallium imaging, an exercise ECG and TEE do not answer this question.
In the picture, the Doberman drives the weak fan while the bat watches whether the stone mouth opens, and the two stones show the two answers.
Memory hook: a weak fan and a stone mouth: let the Doberman pull.
